reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / standard orthopaedic oncology texts
clinicalPearls: A small benign bone-forming tumour, by definition under about two centimetres, most common in children and young adults and predominating in males
The hallmark is well-localised pain that is characteristically worse at night and relieved dramatically by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Typically arises in the cortex of long bones, especially the femur and tibia, with the proximal femur a classic site
Imaging shows a small radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense reactive sclerosis; CT is the best modality to demonstrate the nidus
Spinal lesions may present with painful scoliosis, the lesion sitting on the concave side of the curve
The nidus produces prostaglandins, which explains both the nocturnal pain and its striking response to prostaglandin-inhibiting drugs
Treatment options include conservative management with NSAIDs, since many lesions eventually resolve, or radiofrequency ablation for persistent symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Osteoid osteoma is a benign osteoblastic neoplasm consisting of a small central nidus of woven bone and osteoid set in vascular connective tissue, encircled by a zone of dense reactive sclerosis in the surrounding bone. The nidus is richly innervated and expresses high levels of cyclooxygenase enzymes, generating prostaglandins that mediate the intense, often nocturnal pain and the vasodilatation seen in the lesion. The prostaglandin dependence accounts for the characteristic relief with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The tumour has limited growth potential, does not metastasise, and may involute spontaneously over years.
additionalDifferentials: Osteoblastoma (larger, more aggressive, less reactive sclerosis)
Ewing sarcoma or other primary bone malignancy
additionalInvestigations: Thin-section CT to identify and localise the nidus
Plain radiographs showing a lucent nidus with surrounding sclerosis
MRI to assess marrow and soft-tissue oedema, though it may overestimate aggressiveness
Bone scintigraphy showing focal intense uptake (double-density sign)
Correlation of symptom pattern with response to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Histological confirmation when the diagnosis is uncertain or tissue is obtained at ablation
redFlags: Rapid growth or a lesion larger than expected suggesting osteoblastoma or malignancy
Progressive painful scoliosis or neurological signs from a spinal lesion
Atypical imaging with cortical destruction or a soft-tissue mass
Failure of pain to respond to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, prompting reconsideration
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent; the lesion is benign and does not metastasise, symptoms often settle with medical treatment or spontaneous involution, and targeted ablation is usually curative with low recurrence. Malignant transformation does not occur.
pitfalls: Mistaking the reactive sclerosis for osteomyelitis or malignancy and missing the small nidus
Overlooking a spinal osteoid osteoma as the cause of painful scoliosis in an adolescent
Relying on MRI alone, which can exaggerate surrounding oedema and suggest aggression
Incomplete ablation or excision of the nidus leading to persistent pain
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone
management: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain control, which can suffice while the prostaglandin-driven lesion involutes spontaneously over years
CT-guided percutaneous thermal (radiofrequency) ablation of the nidus as the definitive treatment of choice
Surgical en bloc excision or curettage of the nidus where ablation is unsuitable, such as lesions adjacent to neurovascular structures or the spinal cord
Specific attention to spinal lesions, addressing any associated painful scoliosis
Imaging follow-up for the small risk of residual or recurrent nidus after treatment
Management within an orthopaedic oncology service, with histological confirmation when tissue is obtained
